correctness.rationale: All quantifiers are \(b\ge2,\ m\ge1,\ L\ge2\) for injectively labeled residue clocks. The m-state residue DFAO is accessible, internal, and minimal by distinct current outputs. Incoming labels at matching residue prefixes differ exactly when their positive integer difference is divisible by m but not b. Any such difference along a length-L path is at most \(b^L-b\). Conversely, for b not dividing m, the identity \(m=c(b^{L-1}-1)+t\) with \(0\le c<b\) and \(0\le t\le b^{L-1}-1\) produces a length-L conflicting arrival. The cited shortest-path theorem then gives normalized \(2^{2-L}\); b dividing m makes all arrivals decode their digit as state mod b. Counting nonmultiples of b in the exact L-interval yields \((b-1)^2b^{L-2}\). Executed independent brute-path and witness checks cover 400 (b,m) pairs, finite level spectra, and thousands of constructed words. Finite tests corroborate only; infinite proof is by integer inequalities.

value.rationale: The residue clock is the canonical maximally distinguished m-letter periodic sequence and a natural first family after the source preprint’s period-two example. The theorem classifies every base and period at once; unlike ordinary factor complexity of a periodic word, opacity exhibits exact divisibility-driven transparency and infinitely many dyadic collision-depth transitions. An exact multiplicity law \((b-1)^2b^{L-2}\) gives the size of every positive level set, so the arithmetic result is not an isolated or arbitrary small-\(n\) test. It is not claimed to prove a general result for every periodic coding, and no broader paper-sized contribution is assumed.
